extracted.intended_audience: general readers, DIYers, electricians, electronics technicians, and tool buyers seeking information on diagonal pliers
extracted.subtask_description: A general-purpose encyclopedia entry describing diagonal (wire-cutting) pliers: their purpose, action, common names, safety/insulation, suitable materials, and variations (flush cutters, compound-action, high-leverage designs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended purpose and primary function
rubrics_metrics.description: Pliers intended for the cutting of wire or small stock, rather than grabbing or turning; the cutting edges intersect the joint rivet on a diagonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for cutting wire or small stock and adapted for use in inaccessible places. Emphasizes that these are cutting tools (wire cutters/diagonal cutting pliers), not general gripping pliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting action and blade geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagonal pliers cut by indenting and wedging the wire apart rather than a shearing action; jaw edges are ground to a symmetrical 'V' shape so the two jaws form an 'X' when viewed end-on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blades are made of tempered steel; inductive heating and quenching are often used to harden the jaws. This geometry and hardening determine cutting performance and longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material suitability and jaw hardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Suitability for different wire/material types depends on jaw hardness and overall quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for cutting copper, brass, iron, aluminium and steel. Lower-quality versions are generally not suitable for cutting tempered/hardened steel (e.g., piano wire); attempting to cut such material can indent or break out pieces of the jaws and ruin the tool. Higher-quality side cutters can cut hardened steel (example: 2 mm piano wire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulation of handles (safety/comfort)
rubrics_metrics.description: Handles are commonly insulated with a dip-type or shrink-fit electrically insulating material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insulation provides comfort and some protection against electric shock; indicates suitability for electrical work but does not imply certification or guaranteed safety in all conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flush-cutting variant for electronics work
rubrics_metrics.description: Special diagonal cutters ground flush to the apex of the cutting edge on one side of the jaws to allow trimming wires flush to a solder joint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flush-cutting pliers are used to avoid the sharp tip left by symmetrical diagonal cutters. They are commonly referred to as 'flush cutters' to distinguish them from symmetrical cutters and are preferred for electronics/soldering work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound-action mechanism for larger gauge wire
rubrics_metrics.description: Some diagonal cutters use a compound-action linkage to increase mechanical advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compound-action designs make cutting larger gauge wire easier by multiplying the applied force; useful when manual leverage is otherwise insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Built-in wire-cutter blades and design placements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some pliers for electrical work have wire-cutter blades built into the jaws or on the handles just below the pivot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This design integrates cutting functionality into otherwise multipurpose pliers, offering convenience for common tasks where separate cutters might be unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-leverage and specialized cutting variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations exist that create high leverage specifically to cut through very hard or thick wire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-leverage models are designed for hard wire types such as electrical fence wire, dental wire, and piano wire; selecting such a variant is a quality/fit-for-purpose consideration when very hard materials must be cut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and regional naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional and industry jargon for diagonal pliers varies (snips, nippers, side cutters, diags, dykes, dikes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that terms like 'snips' often refer to larger items and that colloquial verbs ('dike it out') may be used in some trades; correct identification of the tool may depend on regional vocabulary when sourcing or specifying tools.
